There is a commonly held belief in the fitness world that exercises need to be constantly varied to “keep the body guessing” or to “confuse the muscles” in order to make progress. What many fail to realize is that by constantly changing exercises, the body never gets a chance to actually adapt and grow from the stimulus imposed.

Remember that exercise, or more specifically the mechanical tension experienced during exercise, provides the stimulus not the benefit. The adaptation comes about through repeated bouts of a progressively more intense stimulus on specific muscle fibers. And this happens only after an exercise is learned and mastered and properly progressed. Variation lends itself to confusion as well as the inability to accurately chart and record performance, which makes true progression more complicated to achieve.

When new exercises are introduced, many subjects will mistake apparent strength improvements for what is actually a learning effect or neurological adaptations. This learning effect is comprised of general familiarity with the equipment and methods plus increased proficiency in motor skill. This learning effect must be maximized and engrained first before any true muscular strength adaptation can take place. This is the primary reason for the need for non-variation in exercise.

Obviously, there is value for some variation in a workout program. And most subjects will benefit from very slight adjustments in exercises like a gradual increase in the stretched positions or changing the grip/hand position. But what the client should understand is that the basic A routine (generic routine) includes the most effective exercises, involving the largest muscles, most easily learned, and the easiest to standardize and record and therefore progress. It is also the foundation for most advanced level trainees. And the benefit will be more fully realized when the subject learns to perform the exercises with perfect execution, deep concentration, and an ever increasing intensity.

Our "generic routine" is applicable to essentially our entire client base that we will service. This is also known as the "big 5" in our industry and is comprised of a horizontal push and pull (so chest press and compound row), a vertical push and pull (overhead press and pulldown), and a leg press. These five exercises alone will target (and therefore stimulate) most of the major muscular structures of the body, especially for newer trainees. As a subject gets more advanced, a more specialized selection of targeted exercises should be considered including single joint or unilateral movements.

Often a new client will come to MaxStrength Fitness with a goal of either “firming”, “toning”, or becoming more flexible in general or for a specific area of the body. This section is included in the manual to provide the instructor with the knowledge to be able to have an intelligent and informative discussion with these clients.
Firming
For subjects that have a goal of firming up an area, it is important for them to realize that to firm any area of the body requires one or most likely both of these two changes:
Stronger and larger muscles
Decreased body fat

Stronger and larger muscles come about through proper resistance training. A reduction of body fat is almost entirely a dietary issue; yet the general population refuses to give up the notion of exercising for fat loss.
Toning
This word is a form of the proper biological term: tonus. Tonus is the residual tension in a skeletal muscle when at rest. The following statements provide general facts about tonus:
Tonus decreases as a muscle weakens.
And the converse is that as a muscle strengthens, its tonus increases.
Again the case is made as with “firming” that proper resistance training will help to achieve this desired result.
Flexibility

Flexibility is an overrated aspect of fitness. This is because the importance and benefits of muscular strength are underrated, poorly understood, and somewhat feared. But it is unnecessary, even undesirable, to promote flexibility beyond that required for functional motion in daily activity. To reiterate what we learned earlier, although not all exercises provide an extreme degree of stretch, the range of motion over which most exercises are performed greatly exceeds that which the involved joints move through during normal daily activities. Resistance training performed over a full range of motion provides all the flexibility needed for the majority of activities.

This is not to dismiss stretching altogether as there can be a benefit to careful stretching of a chronically tight muscle or muscle group. This can often times provide relief in the moment. But what actually occurs is more of an allowance or tolerance of the muscle to elongate. It is also interesting to note that generally strengthening an area or movement pattern will allow for more apparent "flexibility". This is because the body has become stronger and can achieve those positions or ranges of motion that were not previously attainable due to a lack of strength.
See further insight in the Benefits of Resistance Training module:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ICgOmhQl_tt7xbwr94lzzBN-u203IzgB8zDohvDFFfQ/edit?usp=drive_link

blocks.text: Introduction

If you’ve engaged in a program of fitness that focuses on aerobic activity, such as walking on a treadmill, using an elliptical machine, jogging, spinning, or any low-intensity activity involving the repetitive use of your lower body, you’ve  been wasting much of your time. Or possibly you’ve tried the more full body trends of crossfit, orange theory, or any number of available bootcamps. And while these concepts at least attempt to devote some attention to strength training, they involve a lot of high risk lifts performed in a fatigued state. Not only are these programs not sustainable for most, they can actually be dangerous and injurious. Not to mention that in terms of direct strength training, these methods fall drastically short of optimizing the stimulus as they are geared more toward creating fatigue through discomfort.

For many decades, we have been fed the notion that aerobic conditioning is the answer to all your fitness questions, and that the best way to achieve such conditioning is to engage in steady-state (i.e. cardiovascular) activities. However, this is only one singular factor of physical fitness out of a great many potential benefits of a properly conducted training program. This is also true of yoga, Pilates, and similar disciplines, which tend to ascribe some higher value to extreme flexibility. What  people should seek is a program of conditioning that would involve total fitness, including all of the potential benefits of exercise and not just a portion of those benefits.

At the source of the problem is a serious misunderstanding in the fitness world concerning not only what type of  exercise people should do but also how much time should be devoted to such exercise. An overriding “more is better”  philosophy has been the edifice on which most fitness premises are built. Instead of approaching the solution with a perspective of “how much is necessary” we tend to believe “how much can I handle” will
best provide the results we are seeking. But this philosophy is misapplied because beyond a certain amount, exercise can become detrimental.

Proper exercise, prescribed in the correct dosage, can lead to total fitness. But any amount beyond the minimum  necessary will have a negative result. And as it turns out, the amount of volume of exercise required to produce results isn’t anywhere close to the amount we’ve been led to believe. Especially from the standpoint of strength training.

There’s no doubt that being in good physical condition is an absolute requirement for living an active, healthy, and happy life;  however it is neither necessary nor desirable to do any more dedicated exercise than is minimally necessary to achieve this (we are not referring to recreation here). And the  best type of exercise for this purpose is a progressive, high-intensity, controlled pace strength building exercise program.

One of the keys to productive strength-building exercise is that it must be of a particular intensity level to elicit a meaningful response, or adaptation, from the body. If your exercise intensity is too low, you won’t reach the minimum threshold necessary to stimulate physical changes. Intensity is one of the three key principles of any exercise program, the other two being volume and frequency.

Intensity can be described as the percentage of momentary effort exerted, or more simply, how hard you are working in the moment. Brief activity, causing task failure within 30-seconds to 2-minutes, qualifies as high-intensity. In fact, the more intense the effort, the lower the volume (or duration) of exercise that can be tolerated or that is needed.

The following chart illustrates the inverse relationship between volume and intensity and can be seen as a spectrum of various levels of activity. A single vertical line would indicate an activity with a certain proportion of volume and intensity:
The Inverse Relationship Between Volume and Intensity

The rectangle is divided diagonally with volume in the blue half and intensity in the orange. The vertical lines at either end of the spectrum illustrate the inverse relationship of the 2 principles: more intensity (orange) on the right side and more volume (blue) on the left.

As any vertical line is moved to the left, the less intense the work is and a greater amount of volume will be possible and tolerable. Conversely, if we select a level of effort that is more towards the right side of the spectrum, the intensity of the work is increased, and as a result the volume must decrease accordingly. A common example to help illustrate this premise is to consider sprinting vs. walking. We humans can walk for hours if needed and be able to maintain our pace with almost no challenge. But a true, all-out effort sprint might only last 10 to 20 seconds before our intensity (i.e. output) decreases.

Now, most of us have experienced or can imagine an intense activity where as we reach certain levels of output, our protective instincts ultimately cause us to decide to limit our efforts (i.e. Perception of Effort). Fortunately, with the kind of exercise environment offered by a clinically-styled facility, with medically-based exercise machines, and an instructor qualified to assist your efforts, the risk of potential danger is negated allowing for the kind of intensity described throughout the MSF curriculum (and regular, supervised training will allow us to better tolerate these higher efforts). When we can ensure a high level of safety, along with a high level of efficiency, a high-intensity resistance training program will be the most effective type of exercise for anyone. Strength and muscle are the keys to active longevity and MSF is well-equipped to deliver just that to our communities.

Unfortunately, most people believe that exercise has to be a long and arduous endeavor. Most who attempt to exercise do an excessive amount of volume, they do it too often, and they do not work intensely  enough—i.e. they would fall more to the left side of the spectrum above. This kind of activity is mostly nonproductive, causes harmful wear and  tear, and can be extremely time consuming. In other words, there’s a large investment of resources with very little payoff or return. Realize that not having enough time is the number-one reported excuse for people not exercising on a regular  basis.

Fortunately, when we perform high-intensity exercise, it must also be time-efficient. The more we move toward the right side of the chart above, the higher the quality (intensity) of work and the less of it we can tolerate. As it happens, this kind of  exercise is also the most productive or stimulative. When training properly—brief but intensely—progress should be notable and optimal results should be forthcoming.

In fact, such proper strength training is a powerful therapeutic modality—so much so that it must go through a similar consideration of determining optimum dosage amount and frequency that is used by researchers when developing a new drug. We should  be able to produce a prescription-like recommendation of exercise for the majority of the population, one that can be used to adjust dosage and  frequency for a wide spectrum of subjects, from the very weak to the powerfully strong. But as is commonly experienced in the medical realm, doctors tend to give very broad and under-dosed recommendations for exercise, that often include only walking or basic daily movement.
In order to competently recommend (prescribe) exercise, there needs to be an understanding of the basic biological process of exercise.
The Biological Basis of Exercise

To begin with, we need to consider that the human body is an organism that is able to make adaptive responses to stimuli in the environment. Though exercise is only a stimulus, we tend to think of exercise as something that directly causes a favorable response; i.e., “the abdominal machine will give us great abs.”

In reality, it is the body, not the exercise (or exercise machine), that produces the improvement. In fact, from your body’s perspective, exercise is actually a negative because it threatens our movement.

And movement is our most preserved biological function. As Dr. Doug McGuff likes to remind us, without movement, we cannot get food or keep from becoming food. This is why the body is forced to adapt—it’s a response to something it considers a threat to its survival.
With this basic understanding in mind, here is the simple equation we must consider when determining an exercise prescription:

We should approach exercise from the following biological standpoint: we are trying to create a threatening (but safe) stimulus that will cause your body (a living organism) to adapt and produce a desired response. The response is necessary to protect the organism during possible future exposures to the threatening stimulus.

In the field of exercise, there are many theories as to what approach best produces the stimulus. The most accurate depiction of hypertrophy is best explained by the Stimulating Reps Model of Hypertrophy put forth by physiologist Chris Beardsley. This is the only hypertrophy model that [1] uses well-established physiological concepts (e.g. the size principle, the force-velocity and length-tension relationships, and fatigue mechanisms) to explain how a hypertrophy stimulus is applied to muscle fibers, and that [2] explains all known training variables. See more on these topics here https://www.patreon.com/c/sandcresearch/posts?

Under the stimulating reps model, the key stimulus we seek is mechanical tension. Mechanical tension is produced/experienced by the active muscle fibers in a muscular contraction. Importantly however, it is not enough for a muscle fiber to simply be active to experience stimulative levels of tension.

It is also that the tension results from a high level effort and a slow contraction velocity, which happens as we approach concentric failure on an exercise. With this understanding of mechanical tension, we can standardize intensity. If each subject works to task failure (or as hard as can be expected), we can be  reasonably accurate in our record-keeping and prescribe exercise that is truly progressive and productive.
Our basic equation now looks like this:

In considering this equation, the amount of time it takes for the post-workout fatigue to clear while not extending too far out from the period of elevated muscle protein synthesis (MPS) from the workout dictates an optimum frequency. As stated above, we desire to optimize intensity so that a minimum exercise volume will produce the stimulus, thereby minimizing fatigue. A simple rule to gauge recovery would be whether or not soreness is present (this is to be avoided as it is NOT stimulative) and whether or not progressive overload is occurring at some regular interval. Considering that typical MPS elevations last upwards of 48 to 72 hours [REFERENCE] after a stimulative bout of exercise, and based on the recovery factors discussed above, the stimulus (the relative values of intensity, volume and frequency) can be  conscientiously prescribed.

Importantly, it’s not how much exercise your body can withstand, but rather how much is actually required to affect change. In other words, we want to optimize the timing and magnitude of the stimulus while keeping fatigue to a minimum to ensure recovery.

Since we are attempting to standardize intensity by training to concentric failure, or more accurately termed ‘task failure’, the next  variable to standardize would be the volume of work. As we discussed above, most people perform far too much exercise, and certainly too much to qualify as high-intensity. Remember, the higher the exercise intensity the lower the volume must be.

In general, MSF recommends 5-8 exercises, properly performed on equipment that tracks muscle and joint function. This will usually take anywhere between 20 to 30 minutes. If the intensity of the work is adequate, 5 or so exercises will stimulate most of the major muscular structures of the body. Especially for more novice subjects (by way of Regional Hypertrophy). Advanced trainees will likely require more exercises to better stimulate the different regions of muscle. Each of  the 5-8 sets of exercise will last between 1 and 3 minutes, depending on your experience, age, personality, tolerance, and skill level among other attributes. We use specially designed machines to efficiently, effectively, and safely deliver the stimulus to your body, abiding by the MSF Continuous Tension protocol.

With this protocol, we can standardize the way in which we administer the stimulus and can ensure a level of precision in our  measurements. The Continuous Tension method uses a 6-10 second lifting or positive phase, and  a 6-10  second lowering or negative phase. Ideally, we will use the same pace for both directions, which will result in a smooth, continuous motion. This helps to minimize momentum so that every second of every repetition represents effective and efficient muscular loading. Along with a 6-10 second pace, we use a window of 6-10 repetitions to failure as being the ideal loading for most subjects.
Levels of Strength (Phases of a Repetition)

In attempting to prescribe the intensity of the effort of exercise, we must first understand that there are three levels of strength. Importantly, these levels of strength correspond to the three general phases of a repetition; namely the concentric or lifting phase, the eccentric or lowering phase, and a static or “holding” phase.
These three phases are arranged in hierarchical levels, from concentric being the weakest to eccentric as the strongest.

It may not be immediately obvious but your positive/lifting strength is actually your weakest level of strength. As you perform an  exercise, you will get to a point in the set when you cannot lift the weight anymore. It is at this point (and most often prior to this point) that a majority of subjects will reduce their effort or stop entirely.

And while this can be expected as our protective instincts begin to take over, it by no means signals an inability to continue producing force. In fact this is where it is in the subject’s best interest to begin working even harder to continue positive movement. Once positive movement actually ceases, you’ve only utilized the first level of strength.

At this point, when you can no longer lift the weight concentrically, you can still hold the weight motionless. This is the next level of strength, the static  phase. Again, it’s not something you’d be compelled to do automatically because your body is giving you many signals to  stop, especially as a result of not being able to move. However, your actual strength potential is greater in the static  phase than in the positive phase. Simply, you’re strong enough to continue working to attempt positive motion. This will result in a static effort that comes with more mechanical tension.

When gravity begins to take over and you can no longer even hold the weight in place, you still have the strength to control the weight slowly, lowering without free-falling. This is the negative phase, your strongest level of strength. Rather than  dropping the weight or lowering it abruptly (as your instincts would have you do) you should resist every moment of the  lowering phase, all the way to the end, with all you’ve got. When the negative phase is completed, you’re finally through and have reached the end of muscular failure. And more importantly, you’ve maximized the amount of mechanical tension (stimulus) you can create on that exercise.

Now one of the more interesting elements to this discussion of levels of strength and effort, is that your tolerance to training will improve with practice. Simply stated, you will get better at training with more effort, the more you train, as long as the intent is there.
Strength vs. Resistance (During a Single Set)

This next chart represents a single set of an exercise with an arbitrary 2-minute duration. This graphic representation illustrates the change in our strength and effort over the course of a set of resistance training.

The Duration (the amount of time the set lasts) is indicated by the horizontal X-axis, and Units of Strength are indicated  by the vertical Y-axis. The bars on the graph show the number of units of force from 0 to 100. The grey bars represent the machine’s resistance (selected weight) and the blue bars represent the subject’s strength. Each pairing of blue and grey bars reflect a stage of progression as your musculature progressively fatigues.
Stage 1 - Set begins

At the beginning of the set, the subject starts with a baseline of 100 units of fresh strength (blue bar). The instructor has selected 75 units of resistance (grey bar) on the machine to oppose your strength.

For a stimulative level tension to be created in a reasonable amount of time (and thereby minimizing fatigue), the resistance on the machine must be meaningful. 75-80% of your starting strength capability represents a meaningful resistance. If resistance is too light, the slow-twitch muscle fibers can begin to recover at a faster rate than they fatigue, only prolonging the set and diminishing the stimulus. If resistance is too heavy, there is an additional risk of form discrepancies with excessive loading.

From the starting point, using the MSF Continuous Tension protocol, we aim for a gradual build up of force just to begin the movement. This should take anywhere from 3 to 5 seconds of increasing effort, attempting to apply just enough force to crack the weight stack. This is done primarily for safety but also to take advantage of the sequential nature of our motor unit recruitment pattern (Henneman’s Size Principle).

Once the movement has begun, we will look to move at a slow, controlled pace of somewhere between 6-10 seconds for both the concentric and eccentric phases. Importantly, we strive to keep the same pace at all times in both directions. This is a key component of our protocol and will dictate the required level of effort in the moment (more insight on this in the following stages).
Stage 2 - Strength diminishes

With each passing moment under load, the subject’s strength diminishes by way of increasing fatigue and there are no longer 100 units of strength available (blue bar is slowly dropping). But the subject is still stronger than the 75 units of resistance (grey bar remains the same throughout the set obviously).

After about 60 or 80 seconds, we can expect that the subject has become quite a bit weaker. Instinctively, our bodies try to avoid these situations. The instructor will encourage the subject to work harder in an effort to maintain their pace. In other words, as fatigue sets in, effort must increase proactively to avoid bogging down prematurely. Again, the pace will determine the effort.

Another repetition or so and the difficulty quickly increases as the movement starts to involuntarily slow down. The 75 units of resistance that originally felt moderately heavy, now feels significantly heavier. If the subject is training properly and receiving timely instruction, their effort should approach maximal at this point.
More importantly, we now have the two components required for a stimulative magnitude of mechanical tension-high level of effort with involuntary slowing of the contraction velocity.
Stage 3 - Concentric Failure
As one approaches this stage, and assuming they are properly motivated and their effort is properly directed, it may take upwards of 10 or more seconds to complete the concentric phase of a rep.

Fatigue has mounted to the extent that the subject can now only produce 75 units of force with a maximal effort and the movement ceases. This is concentric failure-the load can no longer be moved in a positive direction. Most training subjects never truly reach this stage as it comes with a certain amount of discomfort and is not instinctively tolerated by the nervous system.
Stage 4 - Set Ends

At this point, strength has dropped to levels below the machine’s resistance, but importantly, the subject’s strength has not diminished completely. It is in the subject’s best interest to continue maintaining the highest level of effort possible. Despite not being able to move the machine, the subject can still continue to add tension to the targeted muscles. Tension does not require movement, only effort.

The instructor will encourage the subject to continue working in a positive direction and then likely begin to count down while the subject uses whatever amount of strength they have remaining. As the subject reaches their maximum tolerable perception of effort, they will work to lower the weights on the negative with as much control as they can muster, creating even more mechanical tension in the process.

In some cases, if the subject has truly used every bit of strength they had during the final concentric attempt, the eccentric portion of the last rep may be hard to control and there is a chance that it nearly gets away from them. This can still be done with control because of the physiological explanation of the levels of strength above.

By using every ounce of available strength on each set and allowing the instructor to guide them through the process, the subject can ensure that a stimulative effort was given, with only one set of exercise. With this approach, we are minimizing fatigue, which allows for more of the body’s resources to be used for building strength and muscle, which is the desired, qualitative outcome. It is not necessarily attached to some predetermined quantitative goal.

This process will be repeated for each of the remaining exercises prescribed in the workout with the highest, qualitative effort, resulting in an optimal stimulus to fatigue ratio being the goal for each exercise.

This high intensity effort represents a serious threat to your body because it is not aware that you are in a controlled, supervised workout environment using resistance machines. For all it knows, you were wrestling with a wild animal for your life. While this may seem extreme, it is nonetheless the reality. To the body, this was all just a stressful metabolic experience, and at the end of that experience it could not move against the resistance. This  becomes a profound stimulus to your body that, if performed consistently over time, will produce an adaptive response.

The response is that the body eventually builds more strength and muscle so that it is more capable the next time the stimulus is presented. Instead of 100 units of strength, your body builds to 110 units. Of course, in expectation of this, the instructor may add more resistance (80 units vs. 75) to compensate for the new strength.

It must be stated here that the increase in resistance is not a requirement. In fact, a stimulus can be created using the same load for an extended period of time. Remember, for a stimulus to be possible, we need a high level of effort combined with involuntary slowing of the contraction speed of the muscle (or slowing of the implement being lifted). What the instructor will consider however, is whether the resistance appears “too heavy” or “too light”. Again, in keeping with our preferred loading parameters, our sets should typically land in the 6-10 repetition range. There is further discussion of these factors throughout our technical manual, the MSF Academy.
The Importance of Recovery Management

The adaptive response to high intensity resistance training is a metabolically expensive one that requires time for the body to replenish the resources that were consumed to make the adaptation. It also comes with a certain amount of fatigue and inflammation that need to clear to give the nervous system the “green light” to permit that required level of effort again. If we administer the stimulus again before your body has completed this process, we will greatly diminish the stimulus, essentially creating more fatigue without the benefit. This requires a judicious approach to exercise programming, which is another competitive advantage of the MSF Continuous Tension protocol.

Knowing this, we can standardize the final element of the stimulus; exercise frequency. As it turns out, the amount of time required to recover sufficiently from a bout of high-intensity exercise is heavily dependent on the volume and specifics of the exercises performed. Under the MSF Continuous Tension protocol, one can technically recover in as little as 24 hours, again depending on the particulars of the work performed. However, in an effort to ensure full recovery and to maximize the timing of the anabolic window, 48 to 72 hours is likely a more optimal frequency. As mentioned above, this coincides with the Muscle Protein Synthesis rate elevation period that is switched on after an intense workout. It represents a period of time that the body synthesizes protein into muscle tissue at an elevated rate.

Activities of lower intensity (jogging, Pilates, typical multiple-set, not-to-failure weight training, etc.) produce a less significant stimulus that is more easily tolerated by the body. In fact, such activities are more similar to the effort required from our daily activities and are heavily dependent on high frequency to maintain. This is why there are different parameters around high-intensity strength training.
Therefore, using intelligent programming, we would consider 50% of the stimulus-response equation as stimulus, and recovery the other 50%. 0% 50%

Importantly, recovery is more than just the time in between workouts. It begins with proper programming of the workout itself. This is another feature of the MSF Continuous Tension protocol-we control volume by performing only one set and those sets are moderately heavy, so as to avoid excessive reps. Additionally, we avoid extreme stretch positions, further reducing potential fatigue mechanisms.

Our bodies do not possess an infinite capacity for tolerating the exhaustive effects of physical stress. On top of that, the older (and less capable) we get, the less recovery ability our body has. In other words, the goal should be to do the most efficient exercise (high intensity, low-volume) so that resources can be used for growth rather than simply recovering to return to homeostasis.

We should also consider that as one gets truly stronger, they will be able to produce an even greater intensity through training and will thus require even more attention to detail in their programming to avoid overtraining.

It is crucial to understand that overtraining is not just an acute interruption in the exercise journey, but can have long term injurious consequences that can set one back years. It will also impact the ability to continue training intensely in the future. Importantly, we must understand that while our strength potential can increase two or three times our beginning levels, our recovery potential does not increase at the same rate and will not reach the same magnitude.

Now that we’ve discussed the effects of exercise on building strength and muscle and the importance of recovery management, let’s look at some of the additional benefits high intensity training provides.
The Body’s Response to High Intensity Training - Additional Benefits
Remember that the body perceives productive strength training as a threat to which the primary response is to overcompensate and grow stronger, but only with proper recovery management.
If this is the case, your body will build muscle and strength to create resiliency to better handle the stimulus the next time it is presented. But the adaptive response doesn’t stop here.

Once a stimulative mechanical tension has been experienced, the body will also respond with a host of other benefits that are at the source of why high intensity training is the most rewarding form of exercise.
The multitude of adaptations that transpire from high intensity resistance training encompass all of what we should expect from an effective exercise protocol and philosophy:
Structural

The process of producing a high level effort against a resistance results in an accumulation of new muscle tissue and an increase in strength. As discussed above, this adaptive response is necessary to create a resiliency in the body to withstand future bouts of effort. In addition to muscle, new bone is added for similar reasons. Bone being living tissue responds to the mechanical loading and hormonal signaling produced by the workout. Further anatomical adaptations include enhanced flexibility, better balance, and improved resistance to injury.
Metabolic

High intensity resistance training creates an environment where growth factors are released and the first stages of muscle growth are stimulated. Further metabolic adaptations include improved glucose tolerance, metabolic rate, and HDL cholesterol improvements.
Cardiovascular System

Your cardio-respiratory system serves the mechanical functioning of the muscles. The higher  the effort of muscular work, the higher the effort of cardiovascular and respiratory stimulus. Further cardiovascular adaptations include improved blood pressure, resting heart rate, and cardiac output.
Hormonal

Quite possibly the most remarkable and impactful of the adaptations to strength training are the ones that influence a positive hormonal change. High Intensity Resistance Training naturally stimulates growth hormone and testosterone, supporting muscle building, fat loss, vitality, and recovery. While those benefits are more obvious, an exciting and possibly unexpected finding is that physical activity is extremely beneficial for improving symptoms of depression, anxiety, and distress. More specifically, a new study shows that physical activity is 1.5 times more effective than counseling or the leading medications[¹]. And while all types of physical activity (e.g., walking, resistance training, pilates, and yoga) were beneficial, higher-intensity exercise had greater improvements for depression and anxiety.

Not to be outdone on the topic of hormones are myokines, and the relatively new understanding of their relationship to high intensity muscular work. In a recent publication of the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, it was noted:

"In the last few years, the muscular system has gained attention due to the discovery of the muscle-secretome and its high potency for retaining or regaining health. These cytokines, described as myokines released by the working muscle, are involved in anti-inflammatory, metabolic, and immunological processes. These are able to influence human health in a positive way and are a target of research in metabolic diseases, cancer, neurological diseases, and other non-communicable diseases. Therefore, different types of exercise training were investigated in the last few years to find associations between exercise, myokines, and their effects on human health. Particularly, resistance training turned out to be a powerful stimulus to enhance myokine release.”
In yet another enlightening article from the peer-reviewed academic journal, Endocrine Reviews, the following benefits of myokines were noted:

"Physical activity decreases the risk of a network of diseases, and exercise may be prescribed as medicine for lifestyle-related disorders such as type 2 diabetes, dementia, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer. During the past couple of decades, it has been apparent that skeletal muscle works as an endocrine organ, which can produce and secrete hundreds of myokines that exert their effects in either autocrine, paracrine, or endocrine manners. Recent advances show that skeletal muscle produces myokines in response to exercise, which allow for crosstalk between the muscle and other organs, including brain, adipose tissue, bone, liver, gut, pancreas, vascular bed, and skin, as well as communication within the muscle itself

As you can see, there are a whole host of expected and unexpected benefits to strength training, of which many of them are the famous Biomarkers of Aging. The more of these biomarkers that worsen, the “older” you are medically. Importantly, the common denominator to all of them is the amount of muscle mass we have, or don’t have. As we get older, we steadily lose muscle (sarcopenia). Without a strength-building intervention, all of these get worse as we age.

So as we can see, physical conditioning with high-intensity exercise can be outright transformative. However, it is important to  understand that it also requires attention to rules and guidelines to make it safe and productive. It takes a collaborative effort between subject and instructor to bring all the elements together so that all of the benefits can be experienced.
General Guidelines
Things We Do To Help Produce the Stimulus
We understand the process in the first place.
We are aware of the biological process of building strength and muscle and we know how to manipulate the variables to produce results.
We make sure the exercise is productive.
We push our clients to train beyond the level that they could do voluntarily, which is necessary as this type of effort goes against our instinctive mechanisms.
We train in accordance with muscle and joint function.

Every muscle has a prime function. When the muscle works in accordance with that prime function, it  can be maximally loaded safely. We customize the settings so that the machine matches muscle and joint function, regardless of the proportions of the subject.
We provide the ideal environment.

An environment between 64 and 67 degrees with low humidity and circulating air allows for the highest level of effort. If body heat accumulates, we experience uncomfortable sensations that will limit our potential output.
We provide privacy.
Productive high-intensity exercise is not a social endeavor. We ensure that when you exercise, you’ll be in a clinically-styled, medically based environment, sheltered from the general public.
We dress professionally.

We dress professionally because we view ourselves as strength training professionals. Productive exercise is a serious undertaking for which we need to be the authority figure. Informal studies have also shown that when instructors are professionally dressed, the subjects they supervise work harder and push themselves more deeply.
Things You Can Do To Help the Stimulus Process
You must be ready to concentrate.
Your body instinctively avoids stressful situations. Only through strict, intellectual override will you be able to train effectively. You must be determined, attentive, and focused.
You must learn to continually train harder.

This takes time, practice, and confidence. Most subjects mistake the sensations of discomfort for failure. As the muscles fatigue, the movement will begin to slow down even more. This sensation is somewhat unnatural and even threatening as we discussed above. It is at this point that most subjects quit or hold the position as the instructor counts them down. Instead, we challenge our clients to really dig deep. It may take upwards of 10 seconds or more to complete the final positive. When failure is truly reached, a subject should not be calmly holding the position during the countdown. Instead, they need to learn how to continue producing the highest level effort possible as if the movement has not ceased. Eventually, the well intended subject will reach a point where the machine will begin to work its way back against their positive effort. This is not easy or desirable to the body and takes months if not years of practice to master. That’s where we come in. MSF instructors understand how to carry out this process safely and efficiently and will help to learn this invaluable skill. But the subject needs to be a willing participant.
You must breathe continuously and freely.

As the work becomes harder, breathe freely without a scheme. This type of ventilation blows off CO2 (carbon dioxide) and keeps your blood pH normal longer. It also allows your muscles to function for a longer duration and therefore experience higher levels of stimulative tension. Avoid breath-holding/Valsalva. Performing Valsalva increases blood pressure along with several other negative consequences. This will be challenging to override however as this is an instinctive mechanism that actually allows us to produce more force in the moment. But it does this to the detriment of the real objective of the exercise.
You must attempt to move smoothly with control.

When subjects are in the more difficult positions of an exercise or close to the end of a set, there’ll be an urge to jab and back off, jab and back off. It’s actually very instinctive to behave in this manner and therefore takes practice to overcome. During  the “back-off” period and before each subsequent jab, there is an unloading effect. This allows the working muscles to regain some of their strength, thus obviating the tension we seek from the training. It also adds an element of risk that is non-productive.
You must understand the objective and purpose.

The assumed objective of exercise is to lift a heavier weight for more reps than last  time. Or to reach some predetermined quantitative measure. The real objective is to subject as many muscle fibers (activate) to as much tension (stimulus) as possible. This requires as high a level of effort as possible with as high a level of quality as possible. Subjects should not necessarily be concerned with quantitative outcomes as that approach will most likely lead to the movement discrepancies we look to avoid.
Things No One Can Do To Help
Genetics play a primary role in the outcomes.

The muscular response to resistance training is genetically mediated and cannot be changed. A multitude of genetic factors help determine the degree of response with the most visible of these factors being the size and formation of the bones and the length of the muscles and tendons. However, among the myriad of complex genetic influences there is at least one recent discovery  that trumps almost everything else we know about the genetic underpinnings of muscular response. Scientists have discovered a gene called myostatin that acts as a “muscular thermostat”, setting an upper limit to the amount of muscle that an organism can grow. When a  muscle approaches the limits of its size, myostatin actually prevents further increases.
So What Does This Mean For You?

We all have a myostatin gene with varying degrees of low, medium or high levels expression. The higher the level of expression, the less muscle mass that can be built. As one becomes stronger, they will produce a degree of muscle growth that allows for an optimal mechanical and metabolic efficiency. While it may not be the amount of muscle desired, it will be the optimal amount for each individual.

But we can all be certain of this: If we use proper exercise to stimulate maximal muscle gains, we will add invaluable tissue that is now being referred to as the “longevity organ”. And if we choose not to incorporate consistent strength training into our lives, we stand to lose out on the benefits discussed throughout this article.
Conclusion

So regardless of the amount of muscle we’re capable of building, or the aesthetic outcome from our training, there’s no arguing that it very well could be the most beneficial and important endeavor we can adopt for our health and longevity. We owe it to ourselves to truly master our training and to be actively involved in our progress. To have qualitative discussions with our instructors about our training and fully optimize our time and investment. Welcome to a new level of excellence in exercise. Welcome to MaxStrength Fitness.

There is a limit to how far a muscle can stretch or shorten. As a result, certain muscles that act on more than one joint (polyarticular muscles) can only effectively produce or allow maximal movement to occur around one of those joints at a time. The ability of a polyarticular muscle to produce or allow movement around a particular joint is called sufficiency.
There are two types of muscular sufficiency; active and passive.

Active sufficiency exists when the body is positioned so all polyarticular muscles required to produce a particular joint movement are at an optimal length to do so. When a polyarticular muscle is already significantly shortened across another joint, it is unable to effectively shorten further to produce the desired joint movement. This is called active insufficiency. An example of this is when the hip is flexed (shortened, therefore “active”) the quadriceps cannot fully shorten enough to completely straighten the knee.

Passive sufficiency exists when the body is positioned so all polyarticular muscles antagonistic to a particular joint movement are at an optimal length to allow that movement to occur. When a polyarticular muscle is already significantly stretched across another joint, it is unable to stretch further to allow the desired joint movement to occur. This is called passive insufficiency. An example of this is when the knee is extended (hamstrings lengthened, therefore “passive”) the hip cannot be flexed as far.
So for practical purposes, consider the following examples:

When performing the leg curl the ankle must be dorsiflexed as the knee approaches full flexion to allow active sufficiency of the gastrocnemius, which crosses both the ankle and knee joints and assists in knee flexion.
When performing the leg extension, the ankles must stay relaxed to allow passive sufficiency of the gastrocnemius so that the knee may fully extend.
Instructors must know how to satisfy requirements for active and passive muscular sufficiency during exercise when applicable.

blocks.text: When introducing the clicker to a client the instructor should inform them of these following two concepts:

1. Obviously there is a quantitative measure associated with the clicker and we record the number of repetitions performed. But what should be emphasized here is that only worthy repetitions are recorded. As discussed throughout the manual, the focus of our protocol is on the quality of the execution not on the weight lifted or the number of reps. Yes, those are important elements but they should never be the concern of the client.

Few, if any, repetitions are ever truly perfect. But within some degree of reasonableness, clients should expect to perform at a certain standard of quality. This will be highly individual based on the abilities and motor skill of the client but the same concept applies. At the very least, all repetitions should be within the 6-10 second window on the positive phase and 6-10 second window for the negative. And all subjects should be held to the standard of performing reps uniformly; meaning, keeping the same pace throughout without any sudden movement or stalling. Add to this the minimum requirement of breathing freely and maintaining a neutral head position (4 "P's") and this becomes the framework for which all clients should strive to perform from a qualitative perspective.

Make them aware that you are only accepting and recording “perfect” repetitions. Let them know that allowing anything outside of these minimum qualitative parameters is potentially unsafe during the actual performance but also from a progression standpoint. If you accept these less than optimal reps, there is a likelihood that they would accumulate enough reps to warrant a weight increase. And with the subpar execution that they are currently using, an increase in weight is only going to exacerbate the situation.

Importantly, we will only record the number of full repetitions completed with acceptable form. In the event that an instructor has a client perform partial repetitions, only those deemed to be full range of motion will be recorded. This is a critical concept to understand because any progressions in load should be based solely on full repetitions. It is therefore imperative for the instructor to observe closely to determine what constitutes a full range of motion for every client on each exercise. This range of motion will likely vary from client to client and from machine to machine.

2. Another and potentially even more beneficial use of the clicker is as an audible command at the upper turnaround. As discussed earlier, there are several instances where the exercise calls for a pause or a squeeze. There are others that require the subject to simply “pass through” the change of direction in a continuous fashion. Often, a subject lingers too long in the upper turnaround of a compound pressing and/or prematurely releases the squeeze of a compound pulling or rotary-form movement.

Over time the client should learn to expect a delayed click and that they should either deliberately pause or actively squeeze depending on the exercise. They will then most likely stay engaged in that part of the movement and subsequently release into the negative better.

As an instructor you will learn to better watch for the squeeze (or pause) and how long to delay the “click”. You will learn to observe the contracting anatomy and the compression of the pads on the movement arm and your timing and cueing will become progressively refined. Do not click until you have instructed and determined that the client has achieved peak force production and has the requisite neutral head and relaxed face and jaw.

In addition to the use of the clicker another important aspect of recording performance has to do with equipment settings and recording results. Consistency among trainers with equipment settings and the standardization of exercise chart nomenclature are required for meaningful comparison and progression of exercise performance between workouts. As part of an instructor’s orientation should be the memorization and understanding of all equipment settings, modifications, and notations on exercise charts.

https://www.latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2024-11-12/slow-motion-strength-training-studios-los-angeles
Here's a relatively recent study showing single set training effective for muscular adaptations. And what's great about this one, it's from the “Pro Volume guys”.
https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/view/484/version/620
Mangine study

Another informative study that is held in very high regard for how it was conducted. Commonly known as the "Mangine Study" as he was the lead researcher. It's hard to find a properly conducted study using trained adults. Anything involving beginners can be deceiving because of the benefit of neural adaptations and the fact that almost anything they do will be stimulative.
Here's a quote from the conclusion:

"The major findings of this study indicated that 8 weeks of high-intensity, low-volume resistance training utilizing long rest intervals stimulated significantly greater 1RM bench press and lean arm mass gains compared to moderate intensity, high-volume program utilizing short rest intervals in resistance-trained men. These results are consistent with previous comparative studies in resistance-trained individuals showing high-intensity programs were more conducive for increasing strength while producing similar magnitude of muscle hypertrophy (Brandenburg and Docherty 2002; Schoenfeld et al. 2014). However, the greater gains in some measures of muscle size observed in INT indicate that high-intensity training may provide a greater stimulus for muscle hypertrophy in trained men."
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4562558/#sec15
Washington Post
https://www.washingtonpost.com/wellness/2025/04/29/minimum-weight-training-per-week/?next_url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wellness/2025/04/29/minimum-weight-training-per-week/
Washington Post - copied to google doc
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yvKNEF-gpV-1-SMe1vmENJtKHA-MamsjWMbgTICpgqQ/edit?usp=sharing
Chris Beardsley Infographic on dose-response relationship of volume:

Fantastic infographic showing the diminishing returns from multiple sets of exercise. Basically, if we count one set as one unit of hypertrophy, it would take 6 total sets to equal two units of hypertrophy. Yes, you read that right, the first set equals one unit of hypertrophy-to get two units of hypertrophy you would need to perform 5 additional sets. And then we’d have to consider how much fatigue that would create and to what degree recovery would be compromised. Regardless, what's important here is the idea that a majority of the benefit is derived from the first set of an exercise and it's not even close. And that's per muscle region...so do one set for upper back and then move on to one set for chest and then hamstrings, etc. The studies are posted at the bottom of the infographic if you wish to look into it.
Myokines and CVD research suggested by Dr. Doug McGuff:
Doug suggested following the research reference links in these papers for the cardiac section specifically for resistance training with hypertension concerns.

OptiTrain study from 2024. Two groups of women with advanced breast cancer that were undergoing chemotherapy. One group performed high intensity strength training and the other did not. Exercise improved the survival and recurrence rate in breast cancer.

Time Magazine: Why Strength Training is the Best Anti-Ager

Global consensus on optimal exercise recommendations for enhancing healthy longevity in older adults (2025) - The Journal of Nutrition, Health, and Aging
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1iYlsGQsaCE3_K4ups2-UZFbX61hmMpNg/view?usp=drive_link
Noteworthy quotes from the study:

“For example, anabolic exercises, such as Progressive Resistance Training, are vital for maintaining or enhancing functional capacity in older adults, particularly those who are frail or with conditions such as sarcopenia and osteoporosis, mobility impairment or those hospitalized or in residential care. This importance is underscored by the rapid loss of muscle mass that older adults experience during hospitalization or periods of illness, leading to weakened muscle strength/power and function, which in turn increases the risk of falls, disability, morbidity, and mortality. No medications currently enhance fitness, functional capacity or alleviate frailty.”  “Despite the numerous advantages of exercise, its integration into mainstream medical practice for older adults remains limited. Most healthcare professionals, including geriatricians, need more training to incorporate exercise directly into patient care. Progress has been made in including exercise counseling for older adults within healthcare settings. Yet, it is often reserved for those without significant physical or mental limitations and generally promotes only mild activities such as walking, often at dosages and intensities not supported by the current evidence. This cautious approach seems to stem from an unfounded fear of exercise-related injuries or the perceived risks of more vigorous activities for older adults, whereas, in reality, sedentariness is the lethal condition. Prescribing non-evidence-based exercise intensifies and/or volumes should be viewed similarly to knowing prescribing sub-optimal medication dosages.”
Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27102172/

Conclusions: When comparing studies that investigated training muscle groups between 1 to 3 days per week on a volume-equated basis, the current body of evidence indicates that frequencies of training twice a week promote superior hypertrophic outcomes to once a week. It can therefore be inferred that the major muscle groups should be trained at least twice a week to maximize muscle growth; whether training a muscle group three times per week is superior to a twice-per-week protocol remains to be determined.
Similar Muscular Adaptations in Resistance Training Performed Two Versus Three Days Per Week
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6724585/
Heavy Resistance Training at Retirement Age Induces 4-year Lasting Beneficial Effects in Muscle Strength
https://bmjopensem.bmj.com/content/10/2/e001899
Muscular Strength and Mortality in Women Aged 63 to 99 Years
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2845052

Conclusion: In this study of ambulatory older women, greater muscular strength was associated with lower mortality even when controlling for accelerometer-measured PA and sedentary time, walking speed, and systemic inflammation. These findings suggest that assessing strength and promoting its maintenance are instrumental for optimal aging.

There are several instances during the course of a workout where there will require a transfer of resistance between the instructor and the subject. These will primarily be the Cervical Extension, Compound Row, Pulldown, Pullover, and Abdominals. These movements require a cooperative technique between the two that must be led and directed by the instructor to ensure a safe transfer of load.

During a loading transfer, the instructor must first bring the movement arm into position, which is usually the midpoint on most exercises. The instructor then guides the client to engage the movement arm with the proper part of the body. After affirming proper alignment with the machine, the trainer will instruct the client to begin applying gradual force to the movement arm while the trainer begins to lessen his or her force. The instructor then gradually “hands off” the resistance entirely to the client and pinpoints the completion of the transfer with a clear, concise signal of “yours”.

This should be rehearsed between instructors as many times as is necessary before it is used with a client to ensure mastery. The movement arm should be held absolutely still during the transfer and the instructor must not give the signal until the transfer is complete. Both of these factors must be understood by the instructor and the client as there is a potential for injury during this action.

After the transfer is complete, the subject begins by moving into the stretch or negative phase of the exercise for most of the movements. The first repetition then begins after the subject has completed the lower turnaround.
Interpersonal Unloading Transfers

The exact same concepts apply as in the loading transfer above except this time the resistance is transferred from the subject to the instructor or unloaded. This technique will most likely only be used on the Cervical Extension exercise; however, it is quite possibly even more important to master for safety purposes.

This transfer should also take place at or about the midpoint of the exercise (i.e. neutral head and neck). The instructor should also be careful not to abruptly take the load from the client but rather gradually transfer it away from them. The signal given as the transfer back to the instructor takes place is simply, “that is…mine”. It is also critical for the instructor to make sure both feet are firmly planted so as not to get caught off-guard during the transfer. You must be mentally and physically active with the timing of the transfer; providing verbal direction and sensing pressure changes in the movement arm.

topics.title: The Physiology of Resistance Training (Developing a Narrative)

blocks.text: Now, before we go any further, just know that I too believed in this faulty “bro science” as most of us did and many still do. As a result, I relied on high volume training for the better part of 20 years before I found MSF and began to leverage the scientific literature available. Additionally, in the interest of full disclosure, I think it’s important to acknowledge that I personally do not dive into and dissect these studies. Instead, I rely on interpretations and meta analyses from trusted physiologists. I look for things that make sense and put them together with other things that make sense to formulate my position. I’m also a huge fan of simplification. While there is a ton of detail to consider as an Exercise Practitioner, and I constantly refer to our need to be detail oriented, it should all be supported by a simple framework. And in this case that simple framework is the physiological mechanisms that create responses or stimuli in the body. These are some of the things that will be discussed throughout this paper.
The Common Beliefs

So in beginning to formulate our narrative I think a good place to start is to dispel some of the more commonly held beliefs about strength training. For one, those with a surface level orientation to strength training will tell you that muscle is built by first being torn down and then rebuilt stronger. This is often the only requirement proclaimed for building muscle. In stating this most popular attribute, they are missing the two other mechanisms that are commonly stated as fact by the more well studied coaches, trainers, or physiologists. Those two other avenues to muscle building would be, metabolic stress and mechanical tension. So here we have it, the three ways to build muscle that has been passed around for decades:
Muscle damage
Metabolic stress
Mechanical tension

And the result of having these three mechanisms available for muscle building is that most of the workouts and strategies have been designed to encapsulate all three. Why not, right? It would seem to make sense that the more poles we have in the water so to speak, the better the chance we have at achieving results. The more muscle we should build and the faster we should build that muscle.

Because of the believed mechanisms discussed above, typical workout strategies would include excessive volume in an effort to capture all of the potential benefits. They would have multiple sets of the same exercises and multiple exercises per muscle group including more stretched positions to create the coveted soreness or damage. They would also include high reps for the metabolic stress “finisher” or “burn” that many believe to be stimulative. And for the last one, mechanical tension, I would venture to guess many would want to include some heavier sets. So when you add all that up, you have a lot of volume. And I realize that “a lot” is a relative term here. A lot of trainees would probably think 10 or more sets per muscle group in a workout is pretty standard.
What We Know to be True

Now that we know the beliefs and how that has shaped the more commonly prescribed workout protocols, let’s take a look at what we now know to be true and how that changes things. First and foremost, there is only one driver of hypertrophy…mechanical tension. The other mechanisms were disproved by testing each one in the absence of mechanical tension and observing the results. In either case, damaging a muscle or injecting it with metabolites, there was no myofibrillar hypertrophy (addition or growth of muscle fibers). In the case of muscle damage, the hormonal response is similar to that from a workout but the result is to simply clear the resulting inflammation from the damage and repair the muscle fiber to its original state. And when a muscle is injected with lactic acid for example, there is no muscular growth. These are both side effects of training but not stimuli for growth. Only mechanical tension stimulates muscular growth.

So the next question we should answer is, what is mechanical tension (MT) and how does it lead to hypertrophy? MT is the physical pulling force experienced by individual muscle fibers. Muscle fibers overlap when they contract and this is accomplished by the actin and myosin filaments sliding over top of each other, or overlapping. In other words, muscles “pull” on bones to move them when they contract and this pulling force is what creates MT. Technically MT will be present in any muscular contraction performed by the body. But if we are lifting a cup of coffee and therefore producing MT, is that really going to make us stronger or build muscle?

The answer to that question is obviously no. So then how does MT actually lead to hypertrophy? The key to this most important question lies in something known as the force velocity relationship of skeletal muscle. Simply stated, as the velocity of movement decreases the force that can be produced increases. There is an inverse relationship. So lifting a relatively heavy weight slowly (low velocity) requires a more maximal force. Importantly, this low velocity movement has to be involuntarily slow. Here are a couple of ways to conceptualize this:

The speed of movement of an implement one is lifting begins to slow down despite the effort to maintain the pace or accelerate. This could happen with any object and in any setting such as freeweights, selectorized equipment, strongman training implements, or a heavy bag of mulch in the back yard. If we cannot lift it any faster, we will have a higher level of MT present.

It could more simply be stated as training to or near muscular failure, which for our purposes happens at concentric failure. The reps closest to the end of a set tend to slow down until the subject can no longer lift the weight. And while many believe that failure occurs when the involved muscles are fully fatigued, that is not the case. This is another fallacy that was never linked to a mechanism. Instead, we reach our maximum tolerable perception of effort via the corollary discharge sent to the brain. It is basically a replicate copy of the central motor command signal sent from the brain to produce the effort. That’s another topic for the future.

The slower movement results from a slower contraction velocity in the muscle. The myosin heads of the muscle fiber pull on the actin filaments and slide past each other as they shorten or contract. Because of this slow velocity, the muscle fiber components stay attached longer rather than pulling and releasing almost instantly as occurs in faster movements. By hanging on longer, there are more connections made, which creates a greater pulling force from the muscle. And this higher level of pulling force is what creates the potential for stimulative levels of MT in the active muscle fibers. That last part is critical and it is a foundational concept to understanding the physiology in strength training. It is that a muscle fiber cannot be stimulated until it is first activated by the central motor command of the brain. This is known as motor unit recruitment (MUR) and the magnitude of our MUR is governed by our effort. The greater the effort the greater the MUR. And one of the more interesting ideas in resistance training is that our highest possible levels of MUR can be increased with progressively higher levels of effort over time. So we can increase our upper limit. In fact this must happen I we are to sustain progress. Just know that in an indirect way, the whole purpose of training is to become better at training; to become more tolerant of training; and to get a better effect from training.

In considering all of the above, we can now have a better understanding of why excessive volume, soreness, muscle damage, high reps, etc. are not only unnecessary but detrimental to the results we seek. The fatigue caused from all of those typical workout attributes compete for resources with the hypertrophy stimulus. There will be a lot more to discuss on this topic too if you are interested. The take home message here is that once we create the stimulus, more reps/sets/tension will not necessarily lead to a larger stimulus. Once a muscle is stimulated, it would be best to move onto training another muscle region (many muscle groups have multiple regions).
How Much is Enough?

At this point you may be wondering how much stimulus we need? Is it one rep? Would it need to be multiple sets? Well, the ultimate test will be whether or not we are progressing in our lifts with the same or better execution (and execution is a form of progression itself). Now, when we train consistently for long enough, meaning several years at least, we can expect progress to begin to slow down drastically. It’s important to keep in mind that progress is never linear. There are ups and downs and stale periods where no progress is made. A more experienced trainee can truly be successful by not getting weaker. And while this may seem like a weak mentality if you think about the following, it brings perspective to the reality of our species. Imagine being as strong at 85 years old as you were at 50. Think about the reality of that and how much progress that would actually be. In this way can think of muscle and strength as a bank account and we want to drive that balance up as high as we can as we age.

For the most part, one “hard” set will take care of the stimulus for that muscle region (i.e. the muscle fibers activated for that movement pattern). Now if we’ve been training for any amount of time, we are likely going to have to take that set to failure; or more accurately, reach our maximum tolerable perception of effort. And even more importantly, we need to voluntarily push harder as the movement arm (or implement) slows down. We need to “prove to ourselves” in a way that we really are pushing/pulling as hard as we can and that the movement is in fact slowing down on us. Once we get really expert at doing this, one set will absolutely work. If someone isn’t quite getting there or prefers to train short of failure [known as reps in reserve(rir)], then two sets can and probably should be performed. But with additional sets comes additional fatigue. Every contraction is fatiguing, even at the lowest levels.
What is the Best Overall Strategy for Resistance Training?

The best strategy then appears to be heavier weight for lower reps taken at least close to failure (0 to 1 rir) for one set. And this approach would best be used as part of a full body workout where we are training as many muscle regions that we can, still perform at a high level throughout the workout, and still recover. This also proves why longer rest periods are likely better for strength and hypertrophy. We want to be able to perform every exercise in our program to the highest level we are capable in that moment. And remember we should see improved progress over the long term not necessarily session to session.

Strength training should not be seen as a cardio workout. Although for the deconditioned, it certainly will. They will likely not be able to recover (i.e. catch their breath) between sets if they are training to a stimulative level. This side effect is a bonus as they will become more cardiovascularly fit over time with our workouts.
How Many Sets (Exercises)?

These full body workouts can be comprised of 6 to 12 exercises (Note: some  may not be able to tolerate more than 5 or 6. Quality over quantity will always be the priority). Some will be able to handle more, and if it is targeting a muscle region not covered by one of the other exercises or you want to devote a little more stimulus to an area that can be a strategy. If this is the case, however,  you should probably lower the intensity on a handful of other exercises to account for it. Remember, we do not have endless growth potential and you cannot force more stimulus into the system. While we do not know how much that might be, our body will often let us know when we are overtraining, so be aware of this possibility and adjust accordingly.
What’s the Optimal Frequency?

The last topic we will discuss here is the idea of the period of favorable hormonal state after a training session that appears to last for approximately 48 hours. This is known as the period of elevated Muscle Protein Synthesis or MPS period. We want to maximize our time spent in an elevated state of MPS because that is when we add contractile proteins to existing muscle fibers (sarcomerogenesis) or build new muscle fiber from those proteins (myofibrillar addition). If we do the math then, in order to optimize, we would want to train every other day. And since hypertrophy is muscle fiber specific, we would want to perform similar (or repeat the same) movement patterns in every workout. At twice a week we will build muscle tissue over time and as low as once per week can build strength for the rest of one’s life. There are certain strategies that we can use here and ultimately end up in the same place in terms of genetic potential for muscle and strength but I made a case for what is optimal, meaning the fastest results without pharmaceuticals.
